en: A Commentary on the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* composed by Ācārya Dharmottara. For every distinguished person indeed performs a praise of their chosen deity at the commencement of a treatise;
so too has this noble Dharmottara done.

Proclaiming his own adherence to the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*), and considering that the accumulation of merit arises from the praise of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and further that the treatise will reach its completion and the exposition will achieve its purpose for others by generating an abundance of merit through the listeners’ engagement preceded by such praise, he has begun the praise of the Blessed Buddha with the words "Victorious" (*jayanti*) and so forth.
By this verse, worship of the Blessed Buddha is performed through hymn (*stotra*).
Because the qualities [of the Buddha] have been specified, praise does not apply to others;
for even praise can lead to the accomplishment of one's own and others' welfare.

First, he demonstrates the Blessed One’s perfection of his own welfare with the verse beginning "Victorious over the calamities of birth" and ending with "Sugata," and he demonstrates the perfection of others' welfare with the verse beginning with "diminishing the darkness of the mind."
The connection is that [the hymns] "conquer" or "bring victory" by means of speech.
To the question "whose speech?", he says:
the word *su-* here signifies "beautiful."
The particle *tiṣaye* (or *tisaye*) signifies both "again" (*punar*) and "return" (*āvṛtti*),
because particles possess multiple meanings.

This is the meaning: "Well-gone" (*sugata*) means one who has gone to what is auspicious, like one of good conduct; "well-gone" means one who has gone to the highest degree, like a perfectly full jar.
The Sugata has gone by way of non-return, like a lamp.
To the question "Of what kind is he?", it says: "Because of his enmity toward passion and the rest.
Passion (*rāga*) is the first among those [afflictions] of which it is the beginning—namely, hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth; these are the afflictions (*kleśas*).
Death is their enemy.

Since all afflictions (*kleśa*) have been utterly consumed by the Blessed One without remainder, and since the Blessed One is therefore an adversary to passion and the like, he is likewise the conqueror of the world—the realm of living beings within the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
By this, the means for the perfection of his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*) is shown.
He states "of the conqueror of the world" characterized by what? He says: "by the calamities of birth," and so forth.
*Vyasana* means the production of misfortune.

The compound is formed by the rule of splitting the *yoga* (separating the grammatical connection) as "the calamity (*vyasana*) in respect to birth (*jāti*)"—that is, a locative compound (*saptamī-tatpuruṣa*).
In this context, "desire" means:
the desire that "May I be a god," or "May I be a human."

Alternatively, *vyasana* is that which is variously (*vividham*) cast or thrown away (*asyate*) in many ways; it is a general term formed with a passive derivation. Subsequently, it forms a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the word for "birth" (*jāti*).
Birth itself is a calamity;
by birth, the calamity is distinguished.
Therefore, because the word "birth" functions as the qualifier, it is placed first [in the compound].
The "continuum" (*prabandha*) of the calamity of birth is its "stream" (*pravāha*). Its "production" (*prasūti*) is its generation or arising.
The "cause" (*hetu*) of that [production] is the world; [the epithet refers to Him] who is the conqueror of that world.
In this regard, the collective meaning is as follows:

because the Blessed One has gone by means of what is excellent and so forth, for that very reason he is free from the distress of passion and the like; and because his afflictions have been utterly consumed, he is the conqueror of the world.
To explain what kind of speech conquers, he says "the darkness of the mind," and so forth.
For the mind— that is, the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*)—
craving and ignorance are indeed its darkness.

Just as darkness, being considered "darkness," acts as an obstruction to objects such as jars by means of its quality of non-transparency, so too does ignorance act as an obstruction by means of its quality of grasping things erroneously.
The state of being thin is "tānava."
From the word *igatta* (meaning "darkness"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it is preceded by a light vowel (*laghu*).
One should understand that *manastamasi tānavaṃ* is either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) or a dissolution of the compound (*vacana-pramātha*).

Thus, the words of the Sugata—whose nature consists of the Tripiṭaka of Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya—triumph, bringing about the attenuation (*tānava*) of the darkness of the minds of all people through the process of hearing, reflecting, and meditating.
Victory, moreover, consists in the overcoming of those heterodox treatises;

for in the teaching of the Blessed One, both the means—characterized by liberation—and the goal are demonstrated as determined by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas their own scriptures lack such valid cognition regarding both means and goal. Therefore, it is the words of the Blessed One alone that are victorious, not those of others; this is the praise of the Blessed One.

With the words beginning "samyagjñāna," he refutes the explanation of Vinītadeva; for the purpose belongs to the subject matter itself, and not to the purpose of the treatise, which is the proficiency in right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
The accomplishment of all human goals is the purpose of that proficiency, which is the thorough comprehension of right knowledge itself.

The accomplishment of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) is the purpose; by that [accomplishment], there would be a "purpose of the purpose," and thus it is refuted by implication that this is the "purpose of the purpose. Now, why is it stated that the subject matter and the purpose belong to the treatise (*prakaraṇa*), and not rather that the body and the purpose belong to the treatise? To this he says, "For it is twofold," and so on.
Since the body of the treatise—that is, the nature of the treatise—is twofold, the qualification "subject matter" (*abhidheya*) has been employed.

One might object: "Just as the purpose of the subject matter is considered, why is the purpose of the word itself not also considered? To this, he says "tatra" and so forth. "For the sake of its comprehension" means for the sake of comprehending the subject matter.
"Sandarbha" refers to a specific arrangement or composition.
By the word "also" (api), the arrangement of meaning is also included.
"Examination" (parīkṣā) refers to that by which something is examined; thus, the treatise (śāstra) is called "examination."
By the sentence beginning with "by this" (*anenetyādi*), [the author] indicates the purpose;
by the sentence beginning with "since" (*yasmādityādi*), he shows the summarized meaning; and by the sentence beginning with "herein" (*atretyādi*), [he shows the connection].
Now, it may be objected: while the subject matter and the purpose are factors for the engagement of discerning persons, the same should apply to the connection and other such elements.

To the question, "Why then are those [other factors] not mentioned?", he says: the meaning is that when this subject matter (*abhidheya*) and its purpose (*prayojana*) have been stated, those others are also effectively stated by implication. For the subject matter itself is a part (*bhāga*) or portion (*aṃśa*) of the whole (*rāśi*), which includes the relationship (*saṃbandha*) and so forth.
The meaning is that he states its purpose.
He demonstrates this:
the purpose of the subject matter itself is indicated directly as the thing to be expressed (*vācya*), whereas the subject matter and the other [factors] are indicated as its qualifiers.
The opponent (codaka), observing that the subject matter and so forth are expressed by the primary [word] through its denotative power, has raised this objection;
the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) has refuted it on the grounds that it follows from the inherent capacity [of the words].
He demonstrates that three distinct meanings cannot be directly shown by a single sentence in the passage beginning with "But this is not," and so forth.

The sentence beginning with "one, however" (*ekaṃ tu*), while primarily stating that there is one [treatise], sets forth the three elements—the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the connection (*saṃbandha*)—through the word "that" (*tat*) and so forth.
He demonstrates the meaning of the individual components by means of analysis (*apodvāra*) in the sentence beginning with "therein" (*tatra*).

Now, one might object: it would be more appropriate to say "the derivation of that is being made" (*tasya vyutpattiḥ kriyate*); why, then, is the causative suffix (*ṇic*) used in the expression "that is being derived" (*tad vyutpādyate*)?
He states its fruit and purpose with the words "and here" (*atretyādi*).
"Here" refers to this treatise; the purpose of the activity of composing and listening to the treatise is considered for both the speaker—the author of the scripture—and the listener.
This is because, in that treatise, there exist for both the speaker and the listener the two activities known as the composition of the treatise and the listening to it.
But why is the purpose of these two—the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the hearing (*śravaṇa*)—considered? To this he says, "For thus," and so forth.

With the words "Therefore, by the Teacher," and so on, he demonstrates the purpose of the operation of both; for in the sentence "since by this [treatise] right knowledge is expounded," the two operations of hearing the instrument enter as that which must be performed in order to accomplish the act of exposition (*vyutpatti*).
And that act of exposition belongs to the author of the treatise alone and not to anyone else; this is indicated by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

For it is [the author's] correct knowledge that impels the students who are being instructed, thinking, "Be instructed in correct knowledge," as he has begun this treatise to act as the instructor himself.
Therefore, the purpose of the operation of the instrument is the instruction of the speaker alone, and not of the vessel or other such objects.
Although without them [the students] there can be no instruction (*vyutpādana*), nevertheless they are not the instructors, because they lack the capacity to impel [the students] toward it.

Regarding the phrase "by the students" and so forth: since the students desire to make for themselves that very instruction imparted by the teacher as their own, and since they are those who must be impelled, this treatise is heard by them;
thus, the purpose of hearing is instruction.

And these two meanings are conveyed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Otherwise, the speaker’s unique activity would not be shown in the students’ acquisition of proficiency, nor their own activity of listening.

For everyone is thus dependent upon an instigator; in the absence of the causative suffix, the students would be non-instigated. Those who are non-instigated are independent, and for those who are independent and do not desire the proficiency imparted by the teacher—
It is established that since hearing is a state of being, how can the purpose of the activity of hearing be considered?

Now, one might object: "Just as the words expressing the subject matter and the purpose are presented separately, why is the word expressing the relationship not also stated? To this he says: "But the word demonstrating the relationship," and so forth.

This very specific topic is the means (*upāya*), which is to be explained by means of the method that will be described as being characterized by ease; the goal (*upeya*) is the thorough understanding [of that means]. Furthermore, the relationship between the means and the goal is precisely the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇasaṃbandha*).
And since this [relationship] is already understood, it has not been stated by means of another word.
And so it has been said: "The treatise and the purpose are indeed [stated];
since the connection is mentioned by way of implication, it is not stated separately from the purpose."

When the subject matter, purpose, and so forth have been stated by such an opening statement, one who considers that [the work] would otherwise be irrelevant to the activity of authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*) raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.
He thinks as follows: "For he who is authoritative proceeds on the basis of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."
Nor does the scripture exist prior to its hearing through the statement of the purpose and so forth in the opening verse, because that opening verse lacks authority.
Its lack of authority arises from the fact that the word has no connection with the actual object [it purports to describe].
By the phrase "by these," [the author refers to] the subject matter and the other [factors].
"By those stated at the beginning of the section" means by those stated at the outset of a portion of the treatise;
"in what has been stated," and so forth—
this is how he thinks.

Even if this initial statement, which establishes the purpose, is not itself a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), it must nevertheless be presented at the beginning of the treatise for the sake of generating doubt regarding its subject matter.

For one who seeks correct knowledge, upon hearing such an initial statement from the author of the treatise, will entertain doubt; and because of that doubt, he proceeds [to study]. This is the intended meaning.

Precisely because doubt regarding the subject matter arises through the initial statement, and because of that doubt one proceeds, it is therefore appropriate for the author of the treatise alone—and not the narrator of a story—to state it.
By this, what was stated by someone—that only the commentators will set forth the purpose and so forth—is refuted.
He demonstrates this with the words "we perceive" (*utpaśyāmaḥ*) and so on;
the meaning is that although there is no direct proof, it is inferred from the composition of this great treatise.

But surely, since there is an absence of any subverting or establishing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one who seeks to produce right knowledge might proceed toward that [object] even without the words of the Teacher, being motivated by doubt; so what is the purpose of stating the opening sentence there?
To this he says: "He thinks as follows:
for [the teaching] is certainly not to be undertaken for one who is undeluded."

For one who, having seen treatises such as the *Kākadattaparīkṣā* which lack a stated purpose and so forth, suspects that this [work] also lacks a purpose and the like, and thus hesitates regarding its uselessness, will not engage with it due to that doubt of uselessness; it is for the sake of such a person that this statement is made. The meaning is that once the words have been spoken by the author of the treatise, a doubt regarding the purpose arises in accordance with those words, and consequently, he engages with it.

He demonstrates the reasons by which a doubt regarding the lack of purpose arises with the words "useless" (*niṣprayojana*) and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning is that, having considered another treatise to be a more concise means than this one, there might be a suspicion that this treatise is not a means due to its lack of essence. Having thus explained the purport of the sentence as a whole, he says "non-contradictory" (*avisaṃvādaka*) and so forth in order to show the meaning of its individual parts.

By stating that "non-contradictory cognition is right cognition" (*samyagjñāna*), the author of the *Ṭīkā* has refuted all of the following: the cognition that merely makes an object known as conceived by the Mīmāṃsakas; the "vision of the object" (*arthadarśana*) as conceived by the Cārvākas; and furthermore, the cognition conceived by some as being "right" even though it is actually erroneous. This is because none of these possess the defining characteristic of right cognition.
How these [other views] fail to be right cognitions has been itself rejected in the *Ṭīkā*.

The opponent maintains that the validity of three cognitions with respect to a single object is established through their respective functions as indicator (*pradarśaka*), motivator (*pravartaka*), and achiever (*prāpaka*).
To refute this, [the author] says: "And when the object has been indicated," and so forth.

When an object has been indicated by the first cognition, which acts as the indicator, and a second cognition subsequently motivates a person toward that very same object, and a third cognition likewise achieves that very same object—therefore...
It does not apprehend more than that which is fit for presentation by way of making it manifest; thus, that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He supports this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth:
[the cognition] does not produce or generate the object, because the object has already arisen from its own causes.
By this, the non-difference between the instigator (*pravartaka*) and the obtainer (*prāpaka*) has been shown.
To demonstrate the non-difference of the instigator from the indicator (*pradarśaka*), he says:

"That very cognition which first arises as an indicator with respect to an object is what makes that object the locus of activity; the meaning is that it renders the object fit to be the locus of activity."
But the second cognition [is not required], because the object of activity has already been made fit for engagement by the first alone.
The word "api" (also/even) refers back to what precedes.
With the words "ata eva" (for this very reason) and so forth, he corroborates his own view with the text of the Master (Ācārya).
From where is this obtained, when at the first [moment] it merely shows [the object] but does not impel or cause attainment;
and at the second [moment] it merely impels but does not cause attainment?
This being so, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that reveals is one thing, while the result consisting of impulsion and so forth is another.
But it is not so;

therefore, what was said is correct. Now, one might object: "Even if the apprehension of the object itself is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, as long as the subsequent two cognitions—the impelling cognition (*pravartaka-jñāna*) and the obtaining cognition (*prāpaka-jñāna*)—do not arise regarding that object, the operation of the means of valid cognition is not yet complete. To this, he says:
"Once [the object] is apprehended," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

"When the object has been apprehended, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is completed; therefore, regarding the establishment of their validity (*prāmāṇya*), [the operation is finished]."
[They are] useless;
therefore, they are not means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
To [the question], "How is the operation of the means of valid cognition completed, or what is that [operation]?", he says:
One's own function (*svavyāpāra*) consists in the production of a certainty regarding one's own object.

And since that certainty has already been produced by the first [cognition] through the apprehension of the object, the function is completed by that much alone, because the person’s purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) occurs on that basis.
Therefore, the second and subsequent [cognitions] have no role here in this same matter.
The meaning is that there is no further operation [of the means of knowledge], because it would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*) since its object has already been attained.
One is said to be "impelled" (*pravartita*) because one is fit for being impelled; one is said to be "caused to attain" (*prāpita*) because one is fit for attaining.

Having thus established, in general terms, that valid cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is that which accords with reality, [the author], demonstrating that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) function as valid cognitions by performing their respective operations in particular, says "In that regard, the object... and so forth.
Among those two, he demonstrates the operation of perception.
"Known as having been seen" means determined as having been seen;
"is followed by conceptual construction" means it is ascertained by a conceptual construction that arises subsequently to that [perception].
This is what is meant.
The meaning is that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it produces a determination of the object as it appears and is non-contradictory.
With the words "But inference... and so forth, he shows the objective domain of activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*) for inference.
The "observation of the mark" (*liṅga-darśana*) refers to the cognition of the mark (*liṅga-jñāna*).

And that is the certain knowledge of smoke as being non-deviant from fire, which is a recollective cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*) that possesses an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum in a general sense.

For example, having perceived smoke through direct perception, there arises a recollection: "In all cases, this [smoke] is born of fire. From that knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*), one ascertains and points out the object of activity.
That inference is the knowledge that arises through a specific relationship, such as the knowledge: "The smoke here is born of fire."
This is what is meant:
the operation of perception, which consists in the production of certainty regarding its own object, is non-different [from the certainty itself].
But for inference, the very arising of the cognition in the form of certainty regarding its own object—following from the observation of the logical mark (liṅga)—is the operation of certainty.
With the words "And thus," and so forth, he clarifies the function of these two.
Therefore, these alone are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By stating that "no other cognition [is such]," he demonstrates the operation of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*): namely, that these two alone are right knowledge and not others, such as verbal testimony and the like, because those do not present a determinate object. Thus, the activity of right knowledge has been shown.
He demonstrates this by stating that "just as these two means of valid cognition [do not produce] knowledge such as doubt, so too [knowledge] cannot be attained" and so forth.
This is what is meant:

Just as perception and inference lead to the attainment of the object presented by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so it is not with doubt and erroneous cognition, because such an object does not exist.

Now, one might object: "Granted that doubt and erroneous cognition lack validity because such an object is non-existent, why then is the cognition 'there is water in this well' not another means of valid cognition?
It cannot be perception, because the water there is beyond the senses."
Nor is it inference, because of the absence of a logical mark (liṅga).
Nor does it have the nature of doubt, because of the absence of both sides [of a dilemma].
Nor is it erroneous, because of the absence of a contrary object.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And by all that is without a mark," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

although a direct cognition of doubt is not perceived here—such as the conceptual cognition "there is water in this well"—nevertheless, [the absence of action] would otherwise occur even without a regulating mark (*liṅga*).
That [cognition] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because it does not definitively determine its object.

Consequently, the meaning of such a cognition would be: "There might perhaps be water in the well. And that which is of such a nature is merely a cognition of doubt (*saṃśayajñāna*), and thus it is not a means of valid cognition. Furthermore, it is established in the *Viniścayaṭīkā* that when one who has acted upon that [doubtful cognition] occasionally obtains water, that [attainment] results from another cognition.

Now, one might object: "Even if doubt and the like do not possess the capacity to lead one to the object as it has been presented, why are they not investigated? To this he says: "And by those seeking purposeful action," and so forth. The intention is that they are useless for the accomplishment of human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

Furthermore, if valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is correct knowledge because it leads to the attainment of the presented object, then [how would you classify] the cognition of yellow in a white conch, the cognition of a jewel in the light of a jewel seen through a keyhole, or the cognition of midday objects at midnight?

Fearing that one’s own cognition might be considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it attains the mere object presented by these [senses]—and that for this reason it would constitute "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*)—he says: "For [cognition] consists in the apprehension of an object," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

[It is not right knowledge] because of the attainment of an object such as the yellow form of a gem situated in the keyhole, which was presented by these [senses], and which is restricted in place and time, such as at midnight.

Because [the object] is attained, and because there is an absence of parts and so forth distinct from space and time, for this very reason these are indeed not means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather they are not correct cognitions (*samyagjñāna*).

As for those which are the objects to be excluded by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), they should have been shown in that very context concerning the introduction of the term "non-erroneous"; nevertheless, since they were mentioned here in the context of discussing what is to be excluded from correct cognition, there is no fault.
[The opponent asks: "But surely," and so forth.
The opponent thinks as follows:

Since that which is restricted by place and form can be apprehended, let it be that [cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*) when there is the apprehension of another form or another place;
however, it is not [invalid] in the case of [another] time, because things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and thus possess a restricted time, which cannot be apprehended [by a later cognition].

And therefore, just as in the case of a truly blue object, the time of apprehension (*grāhyakāla*) for the cognition of blue is one thing and the time of attainment (*prāpyakāla*) is another, yet validity (*prāmāṇya*) still exists despite this difference in time; so too will there be validity for the cognition of one's own son appearing at midnight being attained at midday.
With the words "It is not said," etc., the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) thinks as follows:

It is true that there is indeed a difference in the entity due to the difference between moments; however, the definition of validity is not stated with reference to the moment, but rather with reference to the continuum (saṃtāna).
Therefore, in the case of blue and so forth, that very continuum which is delimited by the cognition of blue is precisely what is attained by it;
thus, the cognition of blue is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
It is not so, however, with regard to one's own cognition of a son who has been presented as distinct in terms of gross temporal divisions.
This is because it is impossible to determine the identity of a continuum based on a difference in the time of attainment.
By stating that "the unity belonging to the continuum is to be understood," he demonstrates the causal relationship between the ascertainment [of validity] and its subsequent activity.
And how does that causal relationship come about? It occurs if validity is established with respect to the continuum, and not with respect to the individual moment.

That which has right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) as its preceding cause—how is it that the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) is used here in the sense of "cause"? To this he says: "from the effect," and so forth.
Why was the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) not used instead? To this he says: "the word 'cause'," and so forth.

"What kind of immediate cause is the cognition that, with reference to which the mention of the 'prior' word was made for the sake of apprehending the separated [object]? To this he says, "It is twofold," and so forth. Now, why is it said that the cognition appearing as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is the immediate cause? For that is not a causal cognition; rather, it is the resultant cognition (*phalajñāna*).

However, it is appropriate to say this: that cognition appearing as a means (*sādhana*), which immediately produces the cognition appearing as purposeful action, is called the "immediate cause" of that cognition of the means.

That very thing is intended here by the term "appearance of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyānirbhāsa*). How so? Causal efficiency is that which appears; it is the manifestation [of an object] as a reflection, namely the arising of a cognition possessing that form. Since this arises from an immediately preceding cognition, that cognition which establishes it is the "cognition of the appearance of causal efficiency," that is, the cognition of the means [to that effect].
In this case as well, the compound should be understood in the same way.

Alternatively, the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) alone is the immediate cause; it is the "indirect" means of knowledge (*sādhana*), appearing as the object to be attained or avoided, which functions as the motivator with respect to the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of performing what is to be adopted or rejected.
To the question, "If that is so, why is it not examined immediately [after the initial cognition]? he says: "For in whichever... and so forth.

Only that cognition which prompts a person toward an object capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is subject to investigation; there is no doubt regarding the cognition of the means (*sādhana*) immediately following it, because immediately thereafter, a cognition appearing as pleasure or pain arises.

Since those two are experienced, it is appropriate to act based on the cognition of the means, and thus it does not require investigation. Alternatively, by this reasoning, the cognition manifesting purposeful action itself is not fit for investigation.
"Arthyate," and so forth. [The form] "artha" is derived from the root *arth* in the sense of "to request" (*yacñā*), with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*).
It should also be understood as "aryate."

Because this term *artha* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), the suffix *thak* (forming *ārtha*) is derived according to the *uṇādi* rules. Vinītadeva’s commentary—beginning with "the object to be abandoned" (*heyortha*)—has been refuted.
For he has explained it thus: by the word *artha*, "purpose" (*prayojana*) is meant; the purpose of a person [is] such things as cooking wood and so forth.
Its "accomplishment" means its completion.
And that is incorrect because the accomplishment of an object, such as the cooking of wood, does not arise from right knowledge;
rather, it arises solely from its own causes, such as fire and so forth.

In Dharmottara’s commentary, however, there is no fault, because he maintains that accomplishment (*siddhi*)—which is practice (*anuṣṭhiti*) directed toward objects to be abandoned or adopted—is preceded by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). He will demonstrate this very point: "The abandonment of what is to be abandoned is [itself] practice.
But one might object: is there not something other than what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted?
It is to be disregarded.
To the question of why it is not mentioned, he says: "And it is not to be abandoned," and so forth. He thinks as follows:
True;
it exists.
However, because it is not to be adopted, it is only to be rejected, and thus it is not mentioned separately.

Therefore, what was stated by some—that there is a description of both the avoidable and the adoptable because they are useful for human goals, whereas there is no description of that which is to be disregarded because it is the opposite—is refuted.
The author explains this very point with the subsequent passage beginning with "the word 'all'. With the following text, he refutes the interpretation of the commentators.
Vinītadeva and Śāntabhadra have explained this doubt as follows. How was it doubted?

They raised the doubt that not all accomplishment of the purpose of abandoning or acquiring results comes from right knowledge alone, but rather that some may occur even from false knowledge by mere coincidence (*kākatālīya*); [the sūtra] has refuted this.
It is true;
however, it is explained in this way:
the word "all" (sarva) [is used].
The word "yaṃ" (which) expresses a mode.
By this, the meaning is as follows: the accomplishment of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) consists of two modes, characterized by the accomplishment of the goals of abandonment and acquisition;
it is characterized by the accomplishment of worldly and supramundane goals, and is for the most part based upon right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
That is refuted,
because the word "all" (*sarva*) must be understood here as signifying totality, in the sense that "everything was created by Brahman."

Therefore, this is the meaning: whatever complete accomplishment of an object—characterized by rejection and acquisition—exists, all of it arises from right knowledge alone, and not from false knowledge, because the attainment of an object is not established through false knowledge.

He demonstrates this very point with the following passage beginning with "even of two kinds. With the words "but this is the meaning," etc., he presents his own interpretation, as opposed to the interpretation of others.

Then, by means of the concluding phrase beginning with "tato yāvat" and so forth, he demonstrates that the very same extent of meaning expressed by the word "eva," used here for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), is precisely the extent of meaning expressed by the word "sarva," used here for the purpose of denoting the whole (*kṛtsna*).

One might object: "Since the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha-siddhi*) is stated by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, and because that [accomplishment] is primary, it is logical that the pronoun 'tat' (in the compound *taj-jñāna*) should be connected to it, not to right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). To this, he says: "Even though... and so forth.
He thinks as follows:
for the referent of a word is twofold—the verbal form and that which is to be conveyed.
The objection was raised with respect to the verbal form, while the resolution was given with respect to that which is to be conveyed.
Since it is precisely right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) that is introduced as the subject to be explained, while the establishment of the other [wrong knowledge] follows from its opposite.
Now, one might ask: what is this "explanation" (*vyutpādana*) of knowledge? Is it the production of knowledge, or the removal of defects, or the description of its own nature?
It cannot be production, for that is accomplished by its own causes alone.
Nor is there the removal of a fault;
for by this section, a fault cannot be removed because it is not an agent [of action], nor can it be made known because the fault does not exist.

Nor is it appropriate to state its own nature [at the outset], because the treatise would then be purposeless; anticipating this objection, he says: "It is being elucidated" by means of the removal of misconceptions.
He thinks as follows:
"The true nature of right knowledge is made known through the medium of removing misconceptions."

"By this section" means that right knowledge (samyagjñāna) is that which possesses the characteristics to be described hereafter, and not that which possesses other characteristics; this is a statement of its own nature.
He demonstrates that very misconception (vipratipatti) in sequence, beginning with "the fourfold number and characteristic," and so forth.
With the words "tathā" and so forth, he demonstrates the refutation of misconceptions regarding the number [of means of valid cognition].
Furthermore, there are various types of misconceptions concerning right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

For instance, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that right knowledge consists of six types—characterized by perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, presumption, and non-existence—along with the etymological explanations of these terms.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that there are four types of valid cognition, characterized as perception, inference, verbal testimony, and analogy;
however, some Cārvākas hold that only perception is valid.
By refuting those views, [the author] shows that [valid cognition] is of two kinds.

But surely, once the definition of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) has been stated, it is appropriate to demonstrate its divisions afterwards, saying, "Right knowledge, characterized in this way, is of two kinds. Why, then, was it shown at the very beginning [as being] "of two kinds"? To this he says, "And when there is a difference in individuals," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

This is indeed true; however, if the distinction in number is not stated there, it is impossible to correctly state the definition of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), because the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is one thing and that of inference (*anumāna*) is another.
But when the distinction in number is stated, the specific definition can be properly stated; therefore, the statement of the distinction in number is itself a constituent part of the definition.
But surely, from the statement "perception and inference," it is already understood that [pramāṇa] is twofold.
For what purpose is the term "twofold" explicitly mentioned? It is said in reply:
The restriction "right knowledge is indeed of two kinds" is intended to exclude [other numbers]; by this, the counts of one, three, or four would be refuted.
For if the number two were not stated, there might be the suspicion that while perception and inference are possible, there may yet be other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By the phrase "that which has gone toward the sense-organ" (*pratigatamakṣam*), he demonstrates that this is a *gati* compound.
Why is this compound not shown as an *avyayībhāva*, namely *pratyakṣam*, in the sense of "toward each sense-organ" (*akṣamakṣaṃ prati*)?
If the *avyayībhāva* compound were to be neuter, then *pratyakṣa* would necessarily be neuter;
consequently, forms such as *pratyakṣā buddhiḥ* (direct perception as cognition) and *pratyakṣo ghaṭaḥ* (a perceptible jar) would not occur.
Instead, one would only find *pratyakṣaṃ jñānam* (perceptual knowledge) and *pratyakṣaṃ kuṇḍam* (a perceptible bowl).

In the compound *gatisamāsa*, however, it possesses all genders. Now, one might object: if the etymology is "that which has gone toward the sense-faculties" (*pratigatamakṣam*), then only that sensory cognition which is dependent on the faculties would be denoted by the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), and not the cognition of yogis and so forth, because those do not depend on the faculties. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And being dependent on the faculties," and so on.

"Inhering in a single object" means that in a single sensory cognition, the properties of being dependent on a sense organ (*akṣāśritatva*) and being a direct manifestation of an object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*) are connected.
By the phrase "characterized by similarity," it is cognition itself that is expressed as characterized by similarity to the object;
it is not mere similarity alone.
Otherwise, it would contradict the statement that "knowledge regarding the object of inference [arises] from a mark possessing the characteristic of being inseparable.
Here too, in the case of the compound *paścānmānam anumānam*, one must first set aside the *avyayībhāva* interpretation as before and instead resort to a *gati-samāsa*.

In the sense that "inference (*anumāna*) is a measurement (*māna*) that has followed (*anugata*)," the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*) is provided as an explanation of the meaning; however, there is no compound within that specific sentence.

The word "ca" (and) conjoins direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) as being equal in strength. As for what was stated by Śabarasvāmin and others—that direct perception is the superior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not inference—and as it was further stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*: "When direct perception is more powerful, how can there be inference?"—that has been refuted because both possess equal strength in their respective functions.
He demonstrates this very point [with the following verse].
By the passage beginning with "yathārthāvinābhāva," the interpretation of Vinītadeva and Śāntabhadra is also refuted.
They have explained it thus: "The mention using different case endings in the phrase 'pratyakṣam anumānaṃ ca' [is intended to show that] perception and inference..."
This demonstrates, by implication, the difference in their objects:
just as the grammatical case-terminations (*vibhakti*) of these two are distinct, so too are their objects (*viṣaya*) distinct.
And this is incorrect because, if the indication were made with a single case-ending, the equality of strength [between the two terms] would not be demonstrated by the particle *ca*.
By the phrase "by the universal *pratyakṣatva*," it is distinguished through that universal because there is a plurality of individual instances of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The phrase "having referred to perception" (*pratyakṣam anūdya*) is the indication of the definiendum (*lakṣya*).
The definition is stated as follows: "the state of being free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) and "the state of being non-erroneous" (*abhrāntatva*) are not [merely] enjoined;

rather, by demonstrating the relationship between the definiendum and the definition through this, the explanation of Vinītadeva—which takes the form of a relationship between a name and the named—is refuted.
For a name cannot possibly correspond exactly to its referent.

For by stating the meaning as it truly is, misconception would be dispelled. Although it is possible to state the meaning as it truly is by means of an etymological definition— namely, that "perception is that which is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous"— nevertheless, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of perception would not have been stated, because...

Furthermore, since perception possesses its own nature, such as the direct apprehension of an object and so forth, when the definition and the definiendum are stated according to their true meaning, they are fully explained.
Whatever is perception should be understood as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
For this very reason, the formulation of the definition does not constitute the creation of a name; for the formulation of a definition is not perceived as having the function of creating a name.

Having restated "sound," its characteristic—impermanence—is prescribed; it is understood that impermanence itself is not the name. Thus, there is a distinction between the name and the formulation of a characteristic.

As for one who, having made a restatement of these two—which are well-established in other sections—prescribes perceptibility, he has in effect described the relationship between the characterized and the characteristic in reverse; for at the time of prescribing a characteristic, the characterized is restated and the characteristic is prescribed, but the characteristic is not restated and the characterized is prescribed.

However, once the relationship between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the defined (*lakṣya*) has been established, the definition is restated (*anūdya*) and the defined is enjoined (*vidhīyate*), as in the case: "He who possesses a topknot is a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).

But at the time of enjoining the definition—the topknot—it is the topknot itself that is enjoined by way of restating the wandering mendicant; there is no contrary injunction. Furthermore, another refutation of this position was provided by the author of the *Ṭīkā* in the *Viniścaya-ṭīkā*, which should be consulted therein.

Now, one might object: since perception (*pratyakṣa*) is as yet unestablished under the view that this is a definition-prescriptive rule (*lakṣaṇavidhi*), it cannot be the subject of a restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, how can the definition be made known by restating the object defined as perception? For example, in the case of "one with a topknot is a wandering ascetic" (*śikhayā pravrājakaḥ*), the definition of the topknot is restated and [the property of] being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and so forth is prescribed. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which for you... and so on. He thinks as follows:

Although perception is not well-known as such by virtue of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), it is nevertheless well-known as perception in its general sense by virtue of being a direct manifestation of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*). For this reason also, it is said that "perception is restated. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since those two [conceptualization and error] are not established, perception itself is indeed unestablished, because perception has those as its intrinsic nature. Anticipating this, he says: "And this should not be thought," and so forth; this is easy to understand.

"Devoid of the nature of conceptual construction" (*kalpanāsvabhāvarahita*) is an expression where the abstract quality (*bhāva*) is emphasized; the meaning is "devoid of the very essence of conceptual construction.

By the statement beginning with "non-erroneous" (*abhrāntam*), which refers to that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*) and not to the form of a real entity (*vasturūpa*), non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) is established.
He shows that the meaning of the term "non-erroneous" is not possible [in that sense] by stating:
"for the sake of non-discrepancy."

When the term "erroneous" (*bhrānta*) is apprehended, he sets forth the subsequent refutation. By the phrase "consisting of phonemes conditioned by arrangement," he demonstrates that there exists no such thing as a shape (*saṃsthāna*) or the like, imagined by others, distinct from the phonemes themselves.

By means of the two terms beginning with "and these two characteristics," Vinītadeva’s commentary—which explains the two terms as serving to exclude misconceptions (*vipratipatti*)—has been refuted by demonstrating the method of exclusion for those two terms.
He, however, has explained it thus:
"Non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) refers to that which is not non-concordant (*avisaṃvādi*).
If this were the case, then even inference would fall under the definition of perception; therefore, the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is included to exclude that.

If it were explained in this way—that "non-erroneous" means that which is not erroneous with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*)—then, since all perceptual cognition is erroneous with respect to its objective support, nothing at all would possess the status of perception. Thus it has been said:
"Everything is erroneous with respect to its object, except for the gnosis of the Tathāgata"—this is the view of the Yogācāras.

However, even that has not been included here by the Master; therefore, that [objection] is untenable, because the Master formulated the two phrases for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions (*vipratipatti*), not for the purpose of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

For this very reason, Dharmottara explained two words while inferring the teacher [Dharmakīrti]. Now, one might ask: "Why does it not serve to exclude [other meanings] even in your own position? To this he says: "And this," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: this word "erroneous" (bhrānta) is not taken in the sense of non-contradiction (avisaṃvāda).
Rather, that which does not err with respect to an object (*ālambana*) that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*) is what is grasped by the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*).
[Objection: But was it not said that the Yogācāra position would then be left uncomprised? [Reply: It is said in response:
There is no fault in the fact that the Master has formulated the definition according to the external system, following the Sautrāntika view.

However, according to the Yogācāra view, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) need not be made, because the subject under discussion is correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), which by its very nature is non-delusive, and there is thus nothing else to be excluded.

Therefore, since inference (*anumāna*) has already been ruled out by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous," the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) serves to eliminate further disagreement regarding the establishment [of the definition].
For this very reason, he says: "but not for the purpose of negating inference.
Furthermore, there is a disagreement on this point;
for instance, the Mīmāṃsakas and others say as follows:

Just as non-conceptual cognition is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), so too is the sensory cognition that joins [the object] with universals (*jāti*) and so forth right knowledge, because it leads to the attainment of the object as it was presented.
Thus they have said:
"Thereafter, however, by means of which [cognition] there is [the joining] with the properties of the thing, such as universals (*jāti*) and so forth..."
That too is determined by the intellect and is thus accepted as being of the nature of direct perception.
And so the grammarians say:
"The denotable object, conjoined with the denoter, appears in sensory cognition;
therefore, it consists of a conjunction with words."
If the eternal nature of wind were to depart from consciousness, there would be no manifestation; for manifestation is that which is characterized by reflective awareness.
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by language.
Likewise, by the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), the position of the Naiyāyikas and others that perception is conceptual (*savikalpaka*) is refuted.

Thus, once non-conceptual perception is established through the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction," the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) becomes redundant; since cognitions such as the perception of two moons have already been excluded from the category of valid cognition (*samyagjñāna*), this term serves solely to refute opposing views.

Likewise, certain teachers (ācāryaikadeśīya) maintain that even the cognition of yellow in a white conch, the cognition of a tree seen while moving, and the cognition of a fire-brand circle (alātacakra) are non-erroneous and constitute valid knowledge (samyagjñāna), because the object itself is not erroneous, whereas the yellow form and so forth are erroneous;
thus there is a disagreement [regarding this], which is now refuted.
By the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), it is established that both [terms] serve the purpose of eliminating misconceptions (*vipratipatti*).
This being so, by the phrase "in the inclusion of the non-erroneous," etc., he demonstrates the subject of misconception regarding the word "non-erroneous.
The intention is as follows: there is no attainment of the tree from that which has been shown to be a moving tree, because of its failure to reach [the destination].
"But from another cognition alone" means from another perception, because of the apprehension of the stable tree.

By the phrase "by the inclusion of the term 'non-erroneous'," etc., he shows that the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is for the purpose of dispelling disagreement (*vipratipatti*). And the object of that disagreement has not been shown by the author of the *Ṭīkā*.
Because it is extremely well-known.

By the passage beginning with "na tv avisaṃvādakam," he demonstrates the fault in accepting that meaning which was previously stated— that the meaning of "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) is not the same as the meaning of "non-discrepant" (avisaṃvāda).

Furthermore, with the words "What kind of conceptualization... and so forth, [the author] asks about the specific type of conceptualization, being ignorant of which one is intended among the many varieties of conceptualization.
For instance, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is sensory consciousness associated with the mental factors of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

According to the view of the Yogācāras, however, with the exception of the non-dual gnosis of the Tathāgata, all cognition is conceptualization when it is discriminated as subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*).
Others, however, state that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is mental cognition associated with genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

By the phrase "associated with verbal expression" (*abhilāpa*), etc., he shows that this refers to conceptualization associated with words, and not to those [associations] enumerated in the scriptures.
For if those were included, the perceptual nature (*pratyakṣatva*) of sensory cognition would be untenable.
By the phrase "that by which something is expressed" (*abhilapyate 'neneti*), he indicates this through an instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*).
Thus, what is intended by the word *abhilāpa* is the signifier (*vācaka*), not the signified (*vācya*) such as the universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth.

Consequently, Vinītadeva’s interpretation is refuted; for his interpretation—that "the expression is that which is expressed" (*abhilapyata ity abhilāpaḥ*), meaning the signified such as the universal—is of such a nature [and thus incorrect].
In this very way, this [definition] must be accepted; otherwise, by means of the mention of "fitness" (*yogya*), that which is fit for connection with a word would not have been stated.
If this were so, then in Dharmottara’s commentary, the state of being connected (*saṃsargabhāva*) of the denotatum—such as the universal (*jāti*) and so forth—would not have been demonstrated.
True, it has not been set forth by him.

By stating that universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth constitute the objective domain (*viṣaya*) within the contemplation of objects, it is effectively stated [by implication] that there is cessation (*nirodha*).

This means a conjunction (*saṃghaṭana*) within a single cognition by way of the forms of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*). Now, one might object: "Even if there is a merging of the two forms within that cognition, nevertheless, there is no relation (*saṃsarga*) between the word and its meaning. To this, he says:
Then, regarding the passage beginning with "when in one," the intention is that even when there is a cognition of the connection between word and object, a merging of their two forms is not possible.
In this context, with the words "there is a certain cognition," etc., [the author] shows the scope of the term "cognizable" (*yogya*).
This refers to the manifestation of two forms in dependence upon one who has mastered linguistic conventions.

Now, for those who have not mastered linguistic conventions—such as infants, the mute, and so forth—it is accepted that there is no association with words in their cognition; therefore, even the state of being expressible by words does not exist for them.
And what is this appearance capable of association? It is the appearance of a word.
However, in the cognition of the mute and others, since there is an absence of linguistic convention, even the appearance of a word is not possible; thus, the capacity for association is also absent.

What is this so-called "fitness" (*yogyatva*)? It is the fitness for establishing a convention regarding the form of the denotable object. Nor is there an appearance of the denotable object in the absence of the delineation of the denotation, nor is there such fitness. Thus Kumārila said:
For there exists first a non-conceptual [cognition] consisting of mere observation,
which arises from the pure object and is similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others.
Then, he presents the opponent's objection—that since there is nothing to be excluded, the term "capable" (*yogya*) need not be employed—by means of the passage beginning with "asatyabhilāpa...
He provides the answer with the passage beginning with "aniyatapratibhāsa...".
He thinks as follows:
What is meant by "being associated with words"? It is simply the fact that conceptual cognition has an indeterminate appearance.
From what is this established? He says: "indeterminate," and so forth.
For that which arises from the object itself necessarily possesses a determinate appearance.
The intention is that it is likewise the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

[Objection: But even conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), when arising from an object, will possess a determinate form; to this he replies with the words "conceptual cognition" (*vikalpajñāna*) and so forth.
The intention is that conceptual cognition arises even without the presence of an object; therefore, only sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) has a determinate appearance.
Conceptual cognition, however, has an indeterminate appearance;
thus, by the words "for even a child," etc., he shows that conceptual cognition with such an indeterminate appearance exists even for children, the mute, and others.

But surely, since an infant lacks proficiency in the articulatory organs such as the palate, there is no utterance of words that possess both general and particular characteristics; so why is it said, "This is that very same [thing]"?
True, it does not exist [in that sense]; however, by the phrase "this is that very same," the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is being described.
By the phrase "this is that very same," precisely the fact of having been previously perceived is expressed.
"With crying ceased" means "one whose crying has departed.
This demonstrates the following.

Even in an infant, there exists conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-vijñāna*) characterized by the reflection upon what precedes and follows, because it functions toward a determined object; just as one who has grasped a linguistic convention acts through the reflection upon what precedes and follows.

And that which reflects upon what precedes and follows has an indeterminate appearance, because the preceding and following [moments] are superimposed [upon it]; thus, since the cognition of infants, the mute, and others is capable of such association, it is established that the term "capable" (*yogya*) must be included in the definition to exclude them.

By means of the passage beginning with "sensory cognition" (*indriyavijñāna*), Kumārila has established that sensory cognition—termed "mere observation" (*ālocana*)—is similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth; in order to refute this, [the author] demonstrates its distinctness under the guise of a conclusion, starting with "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). That sensory cognition which arises by the force of an object and possesses a determinate appearance is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

For this very reason, even though it is admitted that both the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the word and its object possess the relationship of the signified and the signifier, the non-conceptual nature of sensory cognition is established. However, it is settled that while conceptual cognition possesses the signified-signifier relationship of the particular characteristic, it is nevertheless conceptual because the [particular] appears [within it].

By the phrase "even though," he demonstrates the acceptance of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between two particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). According to the reasoning that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the status of being signified and signifier belongs only to universals (*sāmānya*) and not to specific objects or words,
the relationship between the signified and the signifier between two particular characteristics must necessarily be accepted.
Why?

Because, since [the existence of] two universals is already being refuted precisely within the investigation of their objects, the statement here that [perception] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) would be redundant;
for that [statement] also has as its very subject matter the non-conceptual, by way of investigating what is and is not an object.

Thus, that which was asserted by Vinītadeva—namely, that sense-perception is non-conceptual by accepting a general relationship of denoter and denoted (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between two universals (*sāmānya*)—has been refuted through a stylistic turn.

With the words "In that case, auditory perception... and so forth, the opponent demonstrates the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would follow if the relationship of denoter and denoted were applied to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The non-conceptual nature of sensory cognition must be established.
One cannot accept a relationship of signifier and signified between two universals (sāmānya) and then claim that the specific individuality of a word (śabda-svalakṣaṇa) is the signified.

For when the word "pot" or the word "word" apprehends a sound by means of another sound, at that time there would have to be some specific individuality of a word as the signified and some specific individuality of a word as the signifier.

The underlying intention is as follows: when there is hearing of two pure sounds, because both sounds appear in the auditory cognition, the sensory cognition of the ear would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*) due to its having an indeterminate appearance.
This is expressed by the words "even though" (*satyapi*) and so forth.
He thinks thus: [the objection continues].

Although the relationship of signifier and signified exists between the two particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, they do not appear as signifier and signified within auditory consciousness; rather, only the two in their pure state appear. This is because auditory consciousness arises through the power of the proximity of sound, and there is no relationship of signifier and signified between two sounds that are merely proximate.

As long as there is no recollection of the word existing at the time of the convention, how could there be the state of being denoted or the state of being a denoter? To the objection that this [word] will be the denoter through recognition—that "this is that very same [word]"—he says:
"And not at the time of the convention," and so forth.
Because of the difference in their objects, there is a distinction between those two, the former and the latter.
And what is the object of the convention? It is that word which was made the object by the cognition existing at the time of the convention.

And that which was made the object by the previous cognition does not exist now, because, upon the destruction of the previous cognition, the state of being the object of that previous cognition no longer exists.

Therefore, perceiving the state of being an object of a previous time, the non-conceptual [cognition] arising in the present through the power of the sense of hearing is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

If both the word and its referent are grasped simultaneously at one time by the cognition of a yogin and by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), he shows nevertheless that they are grasped by the former because it pertains to a present object, by means of the passage beginning with "the cognition of a yogin.
Now, one might object: even conceptual cognition is empty of further conceptualization; therefore, it too would follow that it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By that conceptualization, by the nature of conceptualization," and so forth. He thinks as follows:
"By the subject (*dharmin*), which is conceptual cognition, [the property (*dharma*)...]"

In this [definition], conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is indicated by its nature, just as "horn-possessor" (*viṣāṇin*) indicates "horn-ness" (*viṣāṇitva*). Consequently, that cognition which is devoid of conceptualization is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Nor is there any fault in saying that conceptual cognition is not devoid of conceptualization.

By placing the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) at the end, [the author] demonstrates that the two definitions—being free from conceptualization (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and being non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)—function as mutual qualifier and qualified, rather than being independent, separate definitions.
The phrase "it connects those two as well" is linked with the subsequent clause, "that [cognition] is a direct perception.
This cause of error resides in the sense faculty itself, because the sense faculty has been overcome by the cataract (*timira*). "Rapid rotation" refers to this.
The exclusion [of certain cases] is by means of the qualifier "rotating slowly.
The phrase "located in the object" is used because objects such as a whirling firebrand (alāta) serve as the cause for the appearance of a circle.
The question regarding "traveling in a boat" concerns the collective whole.
By the words "gacchatyāṃ nāvī" and so forth,
he demonstrates the purpose [of the teaching]:
namely, that [the object] resides in an external locus.
The external ship is the support for service; for one situated therein, the delusion is said to be mediated by that support.
The agitation of wind and so forth, which is the occurrence of a disorder, is the cause of internal delusion.
But is it not the case that the cause of delusion resides solely within the sense faculties?
It is replied:

[the author] says "by all [senses]" and so forth, meaning that it is not the case that one sense undergoes a transformation while others have not reached the object; rather, in the case of *timira* (ophthalmia), it is direct, whereas in the case of a firebrand (*alāta*) and the like, it is indirect. This has been explained in detail in the *Viniścayaṭīkā*.

He shows that [the compound] is a *bahuvrīhi* formed by making a *dvandva* with the word *saṃkṣobha*. However, the intention of the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākṛt*) in the *Viniścaya* is that he forms a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* with the word *saṃkṣobha* and then indicates a *bahuvrīhi-samāsa* with the word "etc. (*ādi*); thus, it is merely a difference in etymological derivation and not a difference in meaning.

When "saṃkṣobha" is taken as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), then, because it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the causes of delusion residing in its substratum, such as wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and so forth, are included; thus, there is no difference in meaning. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of "rapid rotation" and the like? One might ask: why not simply say "timira and so forth" (*timirādi*), since by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), all [causes] will be subsumed?
It is replied: [The text continues: ...it is said.

One might suspect that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), only those factors pertaining to the sense organs—such as cataracts or jaundice—are intended when mentioning "non-slow rotation and so forth.
Therefore, "non-slow rotation and so forth" are specifically included.
If, in including these, the mention of "the path and so forth" were not made, then there would be only the apprehension of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
The inclusion of the phrase "not a characteristic of the mode" and so forth is for this reason.
Therefore, since both [the qualifiers] are employed, it remains established that the totality of both [conditions] is not obtained in cases such as ophthalmia (*timira*).

Although the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) does not appear in the sūtra, there is no fault; for even though error is a property of cognition, by excluding that [error], it is cognition itself that is grasped as perception.

In Vinītadeva’s commentary, there is an explanation of the meaning of the sūtra on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), stating that "direct perception is cognition. Therefore, it is established that non-conceptual cognition is the unerring [form] of direct perception, as opposed to those who postulate the sense faculty itself to be the seer.
By the Vaibhāṣikas, it is maintained that "the eye sees forms."

Since a fault has been raised against mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), [it is argued that] form is seen by two: by visual consciousness and by the mental consciousness drawn forth by it. This mental consciousness, established by scripture (*āgama*), was shown to be perception by the Master Dignāga; however, others such as Kumārila and his followers, being ignorant of its definition, have criticized it.

If that mental cognition (*manojñāna*) operates upon the object of sensory consciousness, then it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended. If, however, it operates upon another object that is spatially remote, how could that mental cognition be either dependent on the sense organ or independent of it? If it were dependent on the sense organ, it would be nothing other than sensory consciousness; if it were independent, then even for one without sense organs, mental cognition would be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which leads to the objection that there would be no such thing as the blind or the deaf.

Furthermore, since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not accepted [by them], the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that cognition is indirect (*parokṣa*), understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), while the object is held to be directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). The Naiyāyikas and others, however, maintain that cognition is apprehended by another cognition, and not through self-awareness, because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself.
The connection [of the sentence] is that "the knowledge of the yogi is not accepted.
The Mīmāṃsakas and others say this:

"Since there is currently no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the existence of yogis themselves, how much less for their knowledge? By the term "dependent on the sense faculties," the four sense faculties beginning with the eye are understood.
The mental faculty (*manas*) is not [the instrument of perception] in that case, because it is being established as self-cognizing direct perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*).

By stating that "perception is cognition dependent on a sense-faculty," the author of the *Vārttika* has effectively declared that the eye is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is the cognition alone— by following its presence and absence— that possesses the capacity for the perception of form and so forth,
and not the eye.

As for what was said—that if cognition perceives, why does it not perceive even that which is obstructed, since there is no impediment for that which is formless?—that is incorrect, because that cognition is produced by an object only when it is in a suitable location, and not by one that is obstructed, as such [obstructed] cognition is not observed.
The explanation of the word "own" (*sva*) is "belonging to itself"; thus, the momentary object belonging to sensory cognition is its own [object].
The explanation of the phrase "immediately following that" (*tasyānantara*) is "there is no interval," and so forth.
The explanation of the word *antara* is "obstruction" (*vyavadhāna*), and so forth.
A homogeneous moment of the material cause (*upādeyakṣaṇa*) that is not separated from the object of the sensory consciousness is called a "homogeneous moment."

And that moment which is to be apprehended is the object (*viṣaya*). By the mention of "object," the immediately preceding light is excluded. The grammatical connection is: "that which has such a [moment] as its cooperative cause" (*sahakārī*)."

But how can the objective moment (viṣayakṣaṇa) be a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), given that the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) cannot exist within a single moment? To this, he says: "And it is twofold," and so forth. He thinks as follows: here, being a cooperative cause does not arise from the state of being a benefactor, but rather from the performance of a single effect.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "viṣaya" (object) and so forth.

"By such [a cognition]" means by a sensory cognition that has its own object as its immediate antecedent and acts as a cooperative condition, serving as the objective support-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
When the yogi’s cognition takes another's cognition of this kind as its objective support, then the yogi’s cognition is produced by that which serves as its objective support.

It is "equal" (*sama*) because the immediately subsequent moment is also a cognition; it is "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) because, according to the rule for *śakandhu* and other compounds, the form of the subsequent member is retained. The phrase "because it is a cause" explains the meaning of the suffix.
By the words "produced by that," etc., he explains this [point].

The meaning is that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is perception only when it is produced by the sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*) acting as its material cause (*upādāna*), with the immediately preceding object of its own [sensory] domain serving as its cooperative condition; it is not produced by [that object] acting as its objective support (*ālambana*).

By the words "when... and so forth, the objection raised by the opponent—taking both [consciousnesses] to have one and the same object—is refuted: the object of the sensory consciousness in the first moment is the object of the mental consciousness in the second moment;
thus, mental consciousness apprehends what was not already apprehended.

Regarding the objection raised by the words "And when... and so forth—namely, that if mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) were not dependent upon the sense faculties, its object would be distinct from the object of sensory consciousness, and consequently there would be no such thing as blindness or deafness, and one could perceive blue and other objects even when obstructed—that has been refuted. This is because the object of mental consciousness is the second momentary object-substance (*upādeya*) which has been grasped [by the preceding sensory consciousness]; therefore, an obstructed moment does not become its object, and thus for those who are blind or deaf, there is no cognition of supersensible things.

It has been refuted [by the opponent] that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not arise from those [sensory consciousnesses] because they lack a cooperative cause consisting of an object immediately following their own object.

However, when it is asserted that [mental consciousness] requires a cooperative cause consisting of an object immediately following its own object, then mental consciousness directed toward sound would not be possible; for no subsequent appropriated moment arises from the sound that is the object of auditory consciousness, since sound is subject to cessation.
Since one sound is not produced from another sound, one must necessarily accept that mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) has sound as its object;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement that "the five external [objects] are cognizable.

By the term "an object immediately following its own object," what is meant is an object capable of being the immediate successor to the object of auditory consciousness, and not merely the moment of the material cause (*upādeya-kṣaṇa*). Therefore, in the location of the object of that consciousness—
When another [sensory] cognition arises, then mental perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa) is produced by the assistance of the object immediately following its own object; thus, there is no fault.
With the words "And this... and so forth, he demonstrates the object of the arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
"When the eye has ceased" means:

When the eye has ceased after having perceived its object, then the visual consciousness that had arisen regarding that perceived object is produced again in the second moment by means of an object immediately following its own object; for there is no activity of the sense faculties therein. Consequently, it is established that mental perception arises through that sensory consciousness acting as a cooperative cause with an object immediately following its own object.

But surely, if its producer exists at a single moment, no purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is obtained therein; thus, because it would be useless for human goals, it would fail to attain the status of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*).
It is replied: the attainment of purposeful activity by those like us does not occur through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), but rather by a yogin who is free from passion and the like.

And at that moment, having apprehended the object presented to the mental [consciousness], they obtain purposeful activity such as the teaching of the Dharma; thus, there is no fault. Now, one might ask: "If the eye is active, why is the arising of the mental [consciousness] not precluded? To this he says, "vyāpāravati" and so forth. The intention is that cognition dependent on all the sense organs is exclusively visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*); there is no arising of a mental [consciousness] [at that time].

Now, one might object: "When the eye is active, sensory consciousness arises in the first moment and mental consciousness arises in the second moment; even though there is no simultaneous arising of two things of the same class," to this he says, "Otherwise," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

When the eye is active, why does sensory cognition (*indriya-vijñāna*) not arise in the second moment, given that the causal conditions are suitable and the object is of a similar nature? How is it that the designation "sensory cognition" applies to those two [moments]? Indeed, if mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) were distinct from sensory cognition and established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception, then its definition would be established by a means of valid cognition; however, since it is not established by any means of valid cognition at all, he says:
"And this," and so forth.
