This kind of [argument], which resembles sensory perception, was presented as a proof for the establishment of mental perception by masters such as Ācārya Jñānagarbha and others, who—while demonstrating through scripture what Dharmottara has established—stated:
"Because of the arising of conceptualization. That [proof] is refuted simply by determining [the meaning] through this very method.
They have explained it thus: when the eye is active, both sensory perception and mental perception arise.

It cannot be said that there is no simultaneous production of two [cognitions], because of the statement: "There is no simultaneous production of six [cognitions] belonging to the same sense-faculties, but there is [simultaneous production] of those belonging to different sense-faculties.
Therefore, there is simultaneous production of two [cognitions] belonging to different sense-faculties.

Nor can it be said that mental [cognition] does not exist there simply because it is not perceived as distinct; for a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of blue arises from a [perception] of the same class.
Moreover, if that [initial perception] were not mental, the subsequent conceptualization of blue would not occur at all.
For a conceptualization arises from a mental self of the same class, and not from a heterogeneous sensory consciousness (*indriya-vijñāna*).
Just as when Devadatta perceives blue, Yajñadatta does not have the ascertainment of blue,
because the continuum of sensory consciousness and the continuum of mental consciousness are distinct;
it is not so with the continuum of mental [sensory] consciousness and the continuum of mental conceptualization, because both lack a sense faculty and are designated as "mental."
To this it is replied:
as for what was stated— that [the universal] exists because of the arising of conceptual cognitions of a similar kind— that proof for its establishment is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
since production from heterogeneous causes is observed through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, when the eye is occupied with its own activity, there is no arising of a mental [perception]; nor is the simultaneous arising of two non-conceptual cognitions of blue observed, because those two are not perceived.

Therefore, since the conceptual cognition arises from the sensory cognition itself—which is of a different class—it does not arise from another conceptual cognition; this is the reason for establishing the existence of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
Moreover, conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions do not belong to separate continua, as is the case with Devadatta and Yajñadatta.

Otherwise, there would be no arising from a non-conceptual [cognition] whose continuum has been interrupted, because those two belong to a single continuum; therefore, the arising of a heterogeneous conceptualization must necessarily be admitted, as the author of the *Vārttika* stated:

"When those very things previously seen are seen again, [the conceptualization arises] through the power of the cognition [of them], by performing its own function, namely recollection," and so forth.
By the term "cognition" (*saṃvit*), only sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*) is meant, not mental [perception].

Consequently, how could the conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) arising through its power be a memory, given that it is of a different genus? Nor is mental cognition referred to as "cognition" in that context, because the validity of sensory perception is what is being investigated in terms of conventional usage.
Furthermore, how can sensory perception possess validity if it performs its own function?
Its own function consists in nothing other than generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding its own object.
Consequently, since a conceptual construction may arise even from something of a different class, this [position] is quite trivial.

One might object: "Since it should have been stated simply as 'mind and mental factors' (*cittacaittā*), the inclusion of the term 'all' (*sarva*) is redundant because there is nothing to be excluded. To this he replies with the words "pleasure and so forth" (*sukhādaya eva*), etc.

The intended meaning is that not only are the well-known pleasure and so forth—both mind and mental factors—perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), but others as well are perceived through self-awareness.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "it does not exist" (nāsti).
The intended meaning is that he asserts the non-existence of a pure state of mind that is unperceived.

By speaking thus, this commentator has shown his intention that there is indeed an absence of pure mind during the state of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), because in that state no state of mind whatsoever is perceived.

For it has been argued: "Indeed, there is no self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself. To this, he says "by which," and so forth.
Since the nature of the self is cognized by this very nature of consciousness (*bodhasvabhāva*), that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is called self-cognition.

He thinks as follows: just as a lamp, by manifesting its own nature as light, does not require another lamp for its own illumination, so too the mind and other such phenomena, by manifesting their own nature as consciousness,
do not require another cognition for their own self-awareness.
Nor is there a contradiction in the capacity for action within itself, since there is no absence of real agency [in this case].
Here too, through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), there exists the relation of object and agent by way of the illuminated and the illuminator.
Even in that regard, the very arising of the form of blue is the illuminating nature of cognition; as for the lamp as well, it is simply its state of existing prior [to the object].
The function of being an illuminator is a secondary conceptual operation.
However, for consciousness, its very arising as having the nature of cognition (*bodharūpatā*) is its self-illuminating character.
Consequently, since consciousness is experienced through direct perception as having the nature of cognition, how can you deny it by claiming that consciousness is imperceptible?
Thus, for the time being, consciousness has been shown to be self-cognizing direct perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) with respect to the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
However, as for the Sāṃkhya who maintains that pleasure and so forth are external forms (*rūpa*), [the author] says to him: "And here, form and so forth are being perceived," and so on.
He thinks as follows:

the internal experience of pleasure and so forth, which is distinct from the blue form and is being experienced through direct perception, cannot be said to be non-different from the external [object] or to possess an insentient nature.
He demonstrates this very point with the passage beginning, "And not the apprehended form," and so forth.
The "activity of direct realization" is the function of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows in its wake.

And since the "smoothness" of the blue object is not apprehended [by perception], the meaning is that the blue object and so forth, as possessing smoothness, are not apprehended by the conceptual construction occurring in its wake.

Therefore, by one who refutes the Sāṃkhya—who maintains that blue and so forth do not have pleasure as their intrinsic nature because they are not established by perception—it has been demonstrated through perception that the apprehended and the apprehender, whose forms are pleasure and so forth, are distinct.
Thus, it was rightly stated by some that an apprehender distinct from the apprehended is not experienced through perception; by this, nothing at all has been denied.
Consequently, all these minds and mental factors are directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
He applies their characteristics with the words "And that," and so forth.
That perception is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), because there is an absence of the application of words and the like therein.
Why?
Because there is no convention with respect to the word;
and that cognition is non-erroneous because it is not inverted regarding its own nature and because there is no sublater [of it].

"Of that which has the appearance of the object being cultivated" refers to [the cognition] grasping momentariness and so forth. "The beginning of the onset of clarity" refers to the commencement of an excellence; beyond that, there is no further excellence for the cognition.
Consequently, the mental consciousness grasping momentariness and so forth, while being cultivated, is slightly incomplete at its final moment.
The ultimate limit of excellence is being described. He demonstrates this very point with the passage beginning, "When there is clarity," and so forth.
Here, under the guise of a conclusion starting with "At the commencement of clarity," he shows the three stages of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the yogi.

The first state is the stage of the excellence of cultivation; the second is the stage of the culmination of that excellence; and the third state is the yogin’s perception of the object being cultivated as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.

By the words "for that appears clearly" and so forth, [the author] shows that even the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the yogin is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), just like sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*), precisely because it possesses clarity.
For an object appears clearly to one who is bound by non-conceptual [perception].

Thus, according to this principle, although both the word and its object are grasped simultaneously by mental cognition (*manovijñāna*) arising at the culmination of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nevertheless, because the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) of both are grasped as being present [to that cognition], the consciousness that grasps them is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Furthermore,

just as mental cognition being cultivated appears as a fusion of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), so too mental cognition arising at the culmination of cultivation appears as the signified and the signifier.
It appears clearly.

Then, because it appears clearly, [the opponent] has raised the objection that the reason "because it appears clearly" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for proving that [cognition] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). To refute this, he begins with the words "For conceptual cognition... and so forth.
He thinks as follows:

although mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) appears as a fusion of the signified and the signifier, nevertheless, in its state of vivid manifestation, that unreal form consisting of the nature of the signified and signifier departs; what remains is its own innate nature as pure experience (*vitti*).

Therefore, that very cognition, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), becomes manifest, and not in the form of the signified and signifier, because those two possess only a superimposed nature.
Otherwise, there would be no clarity in the apprehension of the superimposed form; thus, the reason "because of appearing clearly" (*sphuṭābhatvāt*) is not inconclusive.

However, when conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) apprehends an object capable of being associated with a word, it apprehends that object as having been perceived at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). At that time, the object is not present [to the senses], because there is no such convention regarding it.
And that which was previously perceived was the object of the previous cognition;
yet that previous cognition no longer exists at present—at the time of grasping the object capable of being associated with a word—because cognition is momentary.

Likewise, the status of being the object of the previous cognition also does not exist at present; for in the absence of the cognizing cognition, the object as well—the thing existing at the time of the convention—is absent. Thus, it is not present [at the time of usage].
The conceptual consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*), which grasps by superimposing that object [onto its own form], becomes indistinct;
therefore, clarity is excluded from it and remains only in the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

Therefore, because it is manifest, the non-conceptual cognition of the yogin is non-erroneous; and because it apprehends a pure object through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is consistent with reality (*saṃvādaka*).
The phrase "only this much" means that, starting from sensory perception up to the cognition of the yogin, there is not only sensory direct perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*);
nor is there anything more, since nothing further is perceived.
"Regarding the distinction of types": perception is non-conceptual and non-erroneous with respect to the universal; its "distinction of types" consists in sensory cognition and so forth.
The meaning is: "having established that.
"Regarding the disagreement concerning the object."
In this regard, certain Mīmāṃsakas and others have postulated that perception has both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) as its objects;
whereas inference has only the universal as its object, not the particular.
The Sāṃkhya, however, maintains that the particular is the object of both, since for him the universal does not exist.

Furthermore, for the Vedāntin, the object of both [cognitions] is indeed the universal (*sāmānya*), because everything is one due to the non-duality of the Self (*ātman*), and because both [the cognition of difference and the cognition of oneness] are erroneous with respect to the particular (*viśeṣa*). Thus, there is a disagreement regarding the object of perception and the other means of knowledge.
By the term "particular" (*svalakṣaṇa*), he shows the intended object;
it is that which is real (*tattva*) and which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*).
By this, the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is explained:
that by which burning and other such purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) are characterized is a characteristic.
This he demonstrates.
The unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) alone is the reality (*tattva*) of a thing;

however, the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-rūpa*) is a superimposed form (*āropita-rūpa*), due to the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of non-difference between preceding and succeeding moments.
Therefore, a thing possesses two forms: the unique and the universal (*sāmānya*).

In this regard, he demonstrates that the unique reality (*asādhāraṇatattva*) is the apprehended object (*grāhyaviṣaya*) of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by means of the passage beginning with "that which is unique" (*yadasādhāraṇam*).
Now, why is it called the "apprehended object," given that there might be some other object for direct perception?
He says, "It exists," and so forth, beginning with "twofold.
That which one determines—that object existing in the form of a continuum (*saṃtāna*)—is what is ascertained by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon it.
But how can a continuum be the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), such that it could be the object of a conceptual construction?

It is said: [This is] by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because [the object] is determined (*adhyavaseya*) by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because it has been made an object [of cognition], it is called "the object of perception" metaphorically; thus, there is no fault.
He clarifies this very twofold nature with the words beginning "for another... and so forth.
Furthermore, with the words beginning "likewise inference...", he incidentally demonstrates that inference also possesses a twofold object.
"It is determined as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)" means that it is determined as being capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as burning and so forth.

By the words "that very [object]" and so on, he demonstrates that in the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this is a perception of the object to be grasped (*grāhya-viṣaya*), and not the object to be attained (*prāpya-viṣaya*).
Because there is disagreement among all [schools] regarding the very object that is to be grasped.
What, then, is this object? And so forth. One might think as follows:

Now, an objection is raised: if it is stated that the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of perception, then since the universal (*sāmānya*) is also its object, it too would follow that it is a particular. This is the question.
By stating that "non-proximity" (*asaṃnidhāna*) means "abiding at a distance," Vinītadeva’s explanation is refuted;
for he has explained it thus: "in every respect, the thing..."
The claim that "non-existence" means "absence" is inconsistent,
because if a thing is absent there, cognition itself cannot occur.
Consequently, the distinction between the appearances in cognition is not tenable.
By the words "For that which... and so forth, he demonstrates this:
the distinction between clear and unclear appearance arises solely from the presence or absence of that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and not of a universal (*sāmānya*).

The universal (*sāmānya*) is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because that which is superimposed [as an object] is always indistinct, whether it be far or near. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that it is the universal itself, when perceived from a distance, that has an indistinct appearance, and not the particular characteristic? To this he says, "All [appearances]," and so forth; the intended meaning is that the universal does not exist at all.
Therefore, it is those very particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves that appear clearly or unclearly, not a universal (*sāmānya*).

Now, if the particular characteristic were to have two aspects—clear and unclear—due to being distant or near, then for one standing nearby, there would be two appearances; yet there is no rule that what is clear from afar must necessarily be clear when nearby.
It is said: for a blue object is neither clearly manifest nor unclear; rather, the blue is the nature of blue atoms capable of performing the intended causal function (*arthakriyā*).
The forms of clarity and lack of clarity are produced by adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).
When one perceives blue from a distance, because the light-atoms are overwhelmed by particles of dust, there arises a cognition with an unclear appearance.

However, because of the great abundance of light-atoms (*āloka-paramāṇu*) nearby, those [light-atoms] are not overwhelmed by dust-atoms (*rajas-paramāṇu*); thus, a cognition with a clear manifestation arises.
Through the clarity and so forth of the cognition, the object takes on the forms of being clear or unclear, but this does not occur in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
As for the universal (*sāmānya*), however, it does not possess the forms of being clear or unclear by way of the cognition.
Therefore, that is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Now, it was stated that its object is the particular characteristic; if it is the case that the particular characteristic is the object of perception alone and not of anything else, then inference and so forth would not have the particular characteristic as their object.
Rather, there would have to be some other object for perception.

Now, [the opponent], thinking that if the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of perception and nothing else, then it would not be excluded as the object of inference— and thus inference would have the particular characteristic as its object— asks with the words "Why, again... and so forth, [starting] with "not of inference."
The object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not real. To the question, "How then can it be a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*? he says, "For instance," and so forth.

Although the object of conceptual construction is not a real entity, nevertheless, that very [object] is a particular characteristic because it is determined as having the nature of causal efficiency, such as burning and so on; this is the intended meaning.
"That alone is ultimately real"—
thus he thinks.

For an unreal thing does not become a real thing through the power of superimposition, because that would entail the consequence that everything, such as a rabbit's horn and the like, would be a real thing.
That very thing is the reality (vastu) whose nature is non-figurative; therefore, that alone is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
But is it not the case that even the object of conceptual construction (vikalpa) is ultimately real?
This alone is what is called ultimate existence, namely, appearing in cognition.
Thinking that even a universal appears in cognition and therefore must also be ultimately real, he asks:
"Why, then, is only that [particular] ultimately real?"
With the words "it is sought" (*arthyate*), etc., he explains the meaning of the term "having the characteristic of the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāsāmarthyalakṣaṇatva*).
With the words "this is the meaning," etc., he demonstrates the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the individual words within the compound.
He thinks as follows:
Since that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), the universal (*sāmānya*) is not ultimately real;
for it is of no use in causal efficiency such as burning and the like.
Nor does it possess reality by virtue of appearing [in cognition], because even that which is unreal appears through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Nor does its causal efficiency consist in producing a cognition, because a cognition having a universal as its object arises through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) even without a [real] universal. With the words "From this" (*etasmāt*) and so forth, he shows the object of inference.

With the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth, he demonstrates the dissimilarity between the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—namely, the universal—and the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

But how can a universal (*sāmānya*) be the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? He says: "being superimposed" (*samāropyamāṇam*). The intention is that it is because the form of the universal is cognized as being common to all fires. That [universal] is the object of inference; it is "that which has a graspable form" (*grāhyarūpa*), according to a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has a graspable form. Here too, the object is established in relation to what is grasped (*grāhya*), and not in relation to what is attained (*prāpya*), because there is no dispute regarding the latter.

One might ask: "Since the term *tatsāmānyam* (that universal) was introduced in the neuter gender, how can there be a reference to it by means of the masculine pronoun *sa*? To this he replies with the words beginning "sarvanāmnā" (by a pronoun).

Furthermore, one might ask: "Why did the author of the Vārttika refute the disagreement regarding the object of inference (*anumāna*) in the chapter on perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*), and not in the chapter on inference itself? To this he replies with the words beginning "sāmānyalakṣaṇam. He thinks as follows:
If the object of inference were to be established in the section on inference (*anumāna-pariccheda*), then the discussion should have been composed right there.
What, then, is this object of inference that is distinct from the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*)? And what [is the object] of perception itself?
There would be prolixity if one were to repeat for each of the ten objects that "another [object] must be stated as its specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is stated right here for the sake of brevity.
He says this in order to refute misconceptions regarding the result.
How is there a disagreement regarding the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
For instance, a means of valid cognition is an instrument (*karaṇa*), and it cannot exist without the action of valid cognition (*pramiti*), just as an axe cannot exist without the act of cutting.

Consequently, there must be a fruit distinct from the means of valid cognition—the instrument—characterized by the engagement with the object; for it is a contradiction for something to be both the action and the instrument with respect to itself.
For it is not the case that the axe itself is the act of cutting.

Therefore, the Mīmāṃsaka maintains that the sense organ (*indriya*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as well as the contact between the sense organ and its object, the contact between the mind and the sense organ, and the contact between the self and the mind; indeed, all such contacts are accepted as the means of cognition. As it has been said:
"Or rather, the sense organ may be the means of valid cognition, along with its conjunction with the object."
The connection of the mind with the senses, or indeed of all of them with the self.
Thus, the comprehension of the meaning is the fruit; and because of the operation therein, there is the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

At that time, knowledge is the fruit, and because of the operation therein, there is the status of being a means of valid cognition. When there is no operation on their part, then the fruit is not produced.
Likewise, it has been stated that each preceding [factor] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and each succeeding one is the result (*phala*).
In that context as well, the arising of cognition is the means of valid cognition, while purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth are the result.
Similarly, the Naiyāyikas and others...
They indeed accept the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) as being of this very nature.

However, there is this further distinction: the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is the fruit. As Kumārila has stated:
"The status of being the means of valid cognition and the fruit belongs to the two cognitions of the qualifier and the qualified."
In that case as well, the previously mentioned refutation of the difference in meaning remains applicable.
This is their misconception;
in order to refute it, he says, "That very [cognition].

But how is it that the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the determination of the object, and not the consciousness that prompts one toward the object and so forth? To this he says, "Of the object," and so on.
He thinks as follows:
that very fruit which, once produced, immediately gives rise to the designation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as an instrument is the [true] fruit, and nothing else.
When consciousness has arisen through its capacity to delimit an object, and it produces certainty regarding its own object, the operation of the cognition as a means of valid cognition is completed.
The result is precisely the determination of the object (*arthaparicchitti*), not [the capacity to] impel action and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "this has been stated," etc.

In order to show that the result, which consists of the determination of the object, is distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he again shows the nature of the cognition that is the means of valid cognition—though it was already shown previously—with the words "the cognition that brings about attainment" (*prāpakaṃ jñānam*), etc.
He thinks as follows:

since we accept that cognition which leads to attainment (*prāpaka-vijñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), therefore that power of leading to attainment is nothing other than the determination of the object itself, and not its arising from the object and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "the power of leading to attainment" (*prāpaṇa-śakti*).
Why is it that the mere state of being invariably concomitant with the object does not constitute the capacity for attainment? To this he says, "From the seed," and so forth.

The intention is that since the sprout arises from the seed and other causes as a manifestation of the object, yet the seed and such do not cause its attainment—because a seed remains within a granary and still produces a sprout—the capacity for attainment is distinct from the operation of the cognition's arising from the object.

By the words "Therefore," and so forth, he demonstrates that the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed something other than the operation of the cognition's arising from the object.

Because of the determination of identity between the preceding and succeeding moments, it has been stated that "it is that very same [object]" constitutes the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its attainment upon arising.

If this is so, then if the capacity for attainment is the result, the result would not be of the nature of the determination of the object; for the determination of the object is distinct from the state of being an attainer. To this he says: "And it has been stated previously," and so forth.

It was previously explained in the investigation of the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the very cognition which is the "attainer" (*prāpaka*) is itself the "instigator" (*pravartaka*) and the "indicator of the object" (*arthapradarśaka*).

Consequently, it is established that only the indicator of the object is the attainer; and its power to attain is nothing other than the determination of the object (*arthapariccheda*), since the operation of the means of knowledge is completed by that much alone.
Thus, the fruit of the means of knowledge is precisely the nature of the determination of the object, and nothing else.

Thinking that if the fruit of cognition, which consists of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramiti*), arises from cognition, then there must be a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he asks with the words "If, then," and so forth.
The explanation of the statement "Its similarity to the object is the means of valid knowledge" is provided by the passage beginning with "That similarity which it has with the object," and so on.
He thinks as follows:

The conformity (*sārūpya*) of cognition is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not the sense organs and so forth. By the passage beginning with "For here, because... and so on, [the author] demonstrates that what is produced from an object becomes similar to that object; thus, it is this very conformity, or similarity, that has been described. Now, as for the passage beginning with "But surely...
and so on, the opponent thinks as follows:

We have stated that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and so forth constitute the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); why then would the Buddhist not accept this very same [view], such that he instead maintains that conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition?

Furthermore, if conformity with the object is accepted as the means of valid cognition, then because the means of cognition and its result are identical, the objection raised—that one and the same thing cannot simultaneously be the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*)—remains exactly as it was.
"By virtue of that," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:
"Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is an instrument (*karaṇa*), the most effective among the causal factors (*kāraka*)."

The primary cause of cognition is its very conformity (*sārūpya*) [to the object], because it is by virtue of that conformity that the apprehension of the object is established; it is not the sense organ and so forth, for in the absence of conformity with the object, there is no cognition of the object.
He demonstrates this very point:

By the statement beginning with "the cognition of the object is its apprehension," and by the statement beginning with "for that which has the appearance of blue," [the author] shows that the blue aspect (*nīlākāra*) is the cause for establishing the apprehension of blue within the blue-consciousness.

Since the apprehension of blue is understood when the consciousness possessing the blue aspect is understood, therefore the aspect of the object (*arthākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it possesses the nature of an instrument (*karaṇadharma*).

But surely, consciousness arises from the eye and other [senses], and one indeed perceives a specific object; so how can the form of the object be said to be the most excellent contributing factor? To this he says, "For from which... and so forth.
This explains that even for the eye and other [senses], there exists the status of being a cause for the arising of consciousness.
However, because those [cognitions] serve as causes for the arising of omniscience, they do not serve as causes for the determination of specific objects.
But because the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is unique, it serves as the cause for the determination of specific objects;
that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He refutes the objection raised by others—that because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) are one, there could be neither a goal (*sādhya*) nor a means (*sādhana*)—with the words beginning "And here, [there is no contradiction] between the produced and the producer," and so forth. This contradiction would apply to a single entity only if this relationship between the means of valid cognition and its result were that of producer and produced, or goal and means; what is it then? It is rather the relationship between the determiner (*vyavasthāpaka*) and the determined (*vyavasthāpya*).
From what [source is this known]? From the context of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Because when a specific cognition has arisen, a specific object is made known by the cognizer; the object is not produced [anew].

For instance, when a cognition arises in the form of blue, one establishes a specific knowledge, thinking, "the cognition of blue has been experienced"; thus, it does not produce a [subsequent] cognition.

By the words "something" (*kiñcit*) and so forth, he demonstrates that within a single cognition itself, there exists the relationship of the established and the establisher through the distinction of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitayā*).

Now, one might think: "But how can a non-conceptual cognition, having arisen with a specific form, possess at that very same time the relationship of the established and the establisher through the distinction of part and whole?"
By means of the [passage] beginning with "the established and the establisher," etc.,
and "similar," etc.,
he thinks as follows.
It is not consciousness alone that establishes itself as non-conceptual; rather, it is established by a determinative cognition (*niścayapratyaya*) arising subsequent to perception.

In this regard, the objective form (*arthākāra*) serves as the cause for establishment because it produces the object-cognition through its similarity and exclusion of others; the feeling (*vedana*), however, is that which is to be established.
The determinative cognition, then, is the establisher. This very point is what [the author] demonstrates.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*):

Now, one might object: "The cognition of blue has arisen and is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). If the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is obtained through the force of a determinative cognition (*niścaya*), then it would be appropriate to say that it is 'established by a determinative cognition. However, since a cognition can indeed be a valid means of knowledge even without a determinative cognition, [the author] says 'not established by a determinative cognition' and so forth, thereby demonstrating this."

As long as perception does not produce a certainty regarding its own object—that is, regarding itself—it does not become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it has not accomplished its own function.
Therefore, perception is a valid means of knowledge only when it performs a determinative act (*adhyavasāya*); thus, it depends upon certainty.

Now, one might raise an objection, thinking: "If perception is not even a valid means of knowledge without certainty, then perception accompanied by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would be the valid means of knowledge, and not perception alone, due to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) [of validity with conceptualization]. Thus he objects:

By the words "If it were so," etc., [the author] shows that this is not the case. The meaning is that it is established by means of a determinate cognition (*niścayapratyaya*); however, since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) indeed exists even without a determinate cognition, he says "not established by a determinate cognition," and so forth, to demonstrate this.

As long as perception does not produce certainty regarding its own object and itself, it does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its own function has not been accomplished. Therefore, [the process of] determination...
